name: Fat grafting to chin

card.summary: Using your own fat to build out the chin; a recognized surgical technique in general, but the sources show little chin-specific evidence and the fat can partly resorb.
card.note: Grafted fat can be partly reabsorbed and changes with weight; no chin-specific data in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Fat grafting takes fat from elsewhere on the body, processes it and injects it into an area to add volume. For the chin, it is an alternative to implants or fillers for adding projection or fullness.

The sources reviewed give general information on fat transfer but no chin-specific outcome data.
quick.mechanism: Fat is harvested, prepared and reinjected. Part of it survives as living tissue and part may be reabsorbed, and the result can change with weight gain or loss.
quick.risks: Reported general risks include fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, asymmetry or lumpiness, infection and donor-site pain. It is a surgical procedure performed by clinicians.

lead: Fat grafting to the chin, also called lipofilling or fat transfer to the chin, uses a person's own fat to add projection and fullness to a small or recessed chin. Fat is harvested from another body area, processed and injected into the chin region, so people looking for a larger or more defined chin can use their own tissue instead of an implant or synthetic filler.[1][2]

Fat transfer in general is a three-stage process of harvesting, processing and reinjection, done under local or general anesthesia.[1] The Wikipedia article reports that part of the graft can be reabsorbed, with figures up to 50 percent cited for breast augmentation, and that results can change with weight gain or loss because the transferred fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body.[1] Alternatives for chin augmentation include silicone or porous implants, sliding genioplasty and temporary fillers.[2]

Published studies of fat grafting concentrate on breast, face and scar applications, and no trial specific to the chin was found. Reviews discuss graft retention and the potential regenerative role of adipose-derived stem cells.[3][4]

chain: Fat is harvested from the body
Processed and injected into the chin area
angle.text: The procedure adds volume at the chin using the person's own fat, which is why it is considered for mild recession or contour irregularities. Because the fat is soft tissue, it changes the contour but not the underlying bone.

infobox: Fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes fat transfer as a surgical process that aims to improve areas with irregularities and grooves, and notes its popularity for soft-tissue augmentation in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery.[1] Facial rejuvenation has shifted from mainly removing skin and fat toward restoring volume to deflated facial compartments.[1] A review of lipofilling in the dermatology literature and a surgical review of liposuction both describe fat transfer as used for a wide range of aesthetic and reconstructive procedures.[3][7]

Wikipedia's article on genioplasty describes implants of silicone or porous materials, sliding genioplasty in which a piece of jawbone is moved forward and fixed with plates, and temporary injectable fillers.[2]

Wikipedia says up to 50 percent of transferred fat may be reabsorbed in breast augmentation and that the graft should not be handled too much and should be reinjected quickly.[1] A 2025 scoping review of adipose-tissue staining methods describes tissue viability and matrix composition as factors influencing graft retention.[4] A multicenter randomized trial of fat transfer for total breast reconstruction examined volume retention and confounders of graft survival.[5]

Wikipedia lists fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and cannula injury as complications of fat transfer in general.[1] The Der Chirurg review notes that although liposuction is often presented as minor, it is complex and requires thorough surgeon training.[3]

No studies found specific to the chin. Related research on fat grafting includes the breast reconstruction trial above and a 40-patient trial of fat enriched with adipose-derived stem cells for post-acne depressed spots on the face.[5][6]
